messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Architect
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 70

Ravi is a 41-year-old architect, a South Asian man who has been married to his wife, Anjali, for twelve years. He comes to therapy reluctantly, driven by a colleague’s concern about his withdrawn behavior at the firm. Over several sessions, a story emerges that he has never told anyone.

The abuse began five years ago, during a period of intense stress. Anjali had been under pressure from her family to have a second child, and Ravi’s long hours at the drafting table felt like a refusal. What started as sharp words escalated one night into a slap across his face while he sat at the kitchen table, stunned. He did not fight back—he had never raised a hand to anyone. The next morning, she apologized, cried, promised it would not happen again. He believed her. But the pattern repeated: a shove by the staircase, a thrown glass that shattered against the wall, a kick to his ribs as he curled on the bedroom floor. Each time, he told himself it was his fault—he had provoked her, he had not been attentive enough, he had failed as a husband. The shame kept him silent. In his community, a man does not admit to being hit by his wife. He would be seen as weak, or worse, blamed.

He left after the worst incident, eighteen months ago. She was in a rage, swinging a heavy metal lamp. He shielded his head with his arms, and when it was over, a deep bruise spread across his forearm. The next morning, he packed a bag and moved into a small apartment. He has not told his parents or siblings. They ask why he and Anjali are separated, and he says only that they grew apart.

Now, in his sessions, Ravi’s hands are often clasped tight, knuckles white. He speaks in measured, careful sentences, as if editing each word before it leaves his mouth. He describes nightmares—not of the beating itself, but of being cornered in a narrow room with no door. He wakes in a cold sweat, heart pounding, and sometimes he cannot convince himself that he is alone. He has stopped going to the gym, because the sight of a particular kind of metal weight triggers a visceral memory of the lamp.

At work, Ravi is a senior architect known for meticulous precision. But recently, his focus has fractured. He stares at blueprints for hours, unable to commit a line to paper. He catches himself scanning the office hallway for exits, or flinching when a colleague taps his shoulder. He has started arriving early and staying late, not out of dedication but because the chaos of the open-plan floor feels unsafe. The quiet of his own drafting room is the only place he can breathe. Yet even there, he feels a constant low-voltage dread. He checks his phone obsessively, afraid that Anjali will text—she still does, sometimes, with apologies or accusations. He does not respond, but he cannot block her. He says he is not sure why.

His relationship with his body has changed. He avoids looking at his bruises in the mirror; they have healed, but he still feels them. He shies away from physical touch, even friendly handshakes. When his younger sister hugged him at a family gathering last month, he went rigid and felt nauseous. He has not dated. He tells me he does not trust himself to be near anyone again.

He is not angry at Anjali. He is angry at himself—for staying, for not seeing the signs earlier, for being unable to move on. He says he feels hollow, like a building whose load-bearing walls have been removed. He goes through the motions: attends meetings, submits designs, eats meals, returns to his empty apartment. But there is a fog around him. He cannot remember the last time he felt safe in his own skin. The thought of starting over seems unimaginable. He sits in my office and stares at the floor, his hands still clasped, and says, “I don’t know how to make the fear stop. It’s like the hitting never ended.”
